nodes.title: Christ is the foundation

nodes.displayText: The rock upon which we stand is Jesus Himself.

nodes.title: Getting Christ right
nodes.text: If you've got Jesus wrong, you've got it all wrong.
nodes.notes:
PASTOR SYNTHESIS [279–405s]: Jake expressly teaches that Jesus himself and confession of him as Lord are the foundation of Cedar Grove. INDEPENDENT ANALYSIS [Matthew 16:13–28]: Peter/rock is genuine wordplay; grammar does not by itself exclude Peter; differing traditions assign foundation to Peter, confessed Christ, or Christ himself. JFB says Peter as the heavenly taught confessor; Henry surveys all three approaches. STATUS QUALIFIED. See SPP2 research evidence Matthew 16; retain original teachingStance for Jake’s statement only.

SPP2 v1.1 ADDITIVE SCRIPTURE RESEARCH | Matthew 16:15-19 | publication status: RESEARCH REVIEW, NOT AUTOMATIC PUBLIC DISPLAY
SOURCE TEXT CONTEXT [INDEPENDENT]: Matthew 16:13-28 (Peter’s confession, Jesus’ promise, subsequent rebuke and the suffering Messiah). Audience/genre: Jesus to his disciples, answering Peter; narrative dialogue.
INDEPENDENT BIBLICAL ANALYSIS [NOT PASTOR ATTRIBUTION]: Peter names Jesus as Messiah/Son of the living God; Jesus responds to Peter, promises to build his church, and grants keys. The play on Peter/rock is real and does not grammatically prove that Peter is excluded. Jesus as builder is explicit; the identification of “this rock” has several historically attested readings.
ORIGINAL-LANGUAGE FORMS [PROVISIONAL interlinear cross-check; STEPBible dataset pin OPEN]: Matthew 16:18: Πέτρος (lemma Πέτρος, G4074; noun nominative masculine singular; proper name); Matthew 16:18: πέτρᾳ (lemma πέτρα, G4073; noun dative feminine singular after ἐπὶ); Matthew 16:18: οἰκοδομήσω (lemma οἰκοδομέω, G3618; future active indicative 1st singular)
PASTOR — FAITHFUL AI SYNTHESIS [NOT SPOKEN EXACT]: At 279–405 s Jake states that Jesus himself and the confession of Jesus as Lord, not a human identity, are the church’s true foundation. He treats Christological confession as essential to core values; his sermon does not attempt an exhaustive adjudication of Peter’s ecclesial role.
HISTORICAL COMMENTARY / EXTERNAL COMPARISON [ATTRIBUTED, EDITION/DATASET VERIFICATION OPEN]: JFB relates the rock to Peter as the heaven-taught confessor, while refusing a merely individual-person basis. Matthew Henry surveys Peter, Christ and confession interpretations, endorsing the confession/Christ reading in his treatment. Both acknowledge more than a simplistic petros/petra size distinction.
ASSESSMENT [REVIEW]: QUALIFIED: Jake’s Christ-centered theological application is consistent with 1 Corinthians 3:11 and Ephesians 2:20, but the grammar alone does not rule out Peter’s role in this Matthean saying.
INTERPRETIVE / RIGHTS GATE: Do not imply Koine Greek automatically settles the Peter-versus-Christ interpretation; do not assign any Papal-succession position to Jake from this sermon.
ORIGINAL PPTX SOURCE SLIDE EVIDENCE: 5; 6; 8; original slide associations/timings are unchanged.
ORIGINAL SRT MEDIA EVIDENCE: 243.366; 405.6 seconds; exact spoken wording resides in authoritative SRT, not this synthesis.

nodes.title: Love others unconditionally
nodes.summary: The first relationship is with others: love people in the condition they are in, following Christ's example, without confusing love with approval of sin.
nodes.notes:
PASTOR SYNTHESIS [699–1473s]: Jake links Jesus’ sacrificial love (John 15), love of sinners (Romans 5), divine initiative (Ephesians 2), and active selfless love (1 Cor 13). INDEPENDENT ANALYSIS: John 15 initially addresses disciples; Romans 5 describes God acting while we were sinners, and 1 Cor 13 addresses Corinthian gifts and rivalries. Neither love nor truth authorizes automatically harsh rebuke. STATUS SUPPORTED WITH CONTEXT.

SPP2 v1.1 ADDITIVE SCRIPTURE RESEARCH | John 15:12-13 | publication status: RESEARCH REVIEW, NOT AUTOMATIC PUBLIC DISPLAY
SOURCE TEXT CONTEXT [INDEPENDENT]: John 15:1-17; abiding, love, obedience, fruit and friendship, within Jesus’ farewell teaching. Audience/genre: Jesus to the disciples.
INDEPENDENT BIBLICAL ANALYSIS [NOT PASTOR ATTRIBUTION]: The plural subjunctive ἀγαπᾶτε follows ἵνα within Jesus’ command; the pattern is Jesus’ prior love, concretely self-giving in vv. 12–13. The immediate audience is fellow disciples, though wider Christian love is biblically supported elsewhere.
ORIGINAL-LANGUAGE FORMS [PROVISIONAL interlinear cross-check; STEPBible dataset pin OPEN]: John 15:12: ἀγαπᾶτε (lemma ἀγαπάω, G25; present active subjunctive 2nd plural (ἵνα clause)); John 15:12: ἠγάπησα (lemma ἀγαπάω, G25; aorist active indicative 1st singular)
PASTOR — FAITHFUL AI SYNTHESIS [NOT SPOKEN EXACT]: At 949–970 s Jake reads Jesus’ command, asks what loving in someone’s condition means, and moves to Romans 5:8 to show Christ’s love before moral improvement.
HISTORICAL COMMENTARY / EXTERNAL COMPARISON [ATTRIBUTED, EDITION/DATASET VERIFICATION OPEN]: JFB emphasizes laying down life as the utmost expression of love; compare Matthew Henry’s emphasis on abiding love and obedience.
ASSESSMENT [REVIEW]: SUPPORTED; qualify that “love others in their present condition” is Jake’s synthesis and application, not the dictionary definition of ἀγαπάω.
INTERPRETIVE / RIGHTS GATE: Do not flatten love into unconditional acceptance of conduct, or read a lexical sense that overrides discourse context.
ORIGINAL PPTX SOURCE SLIDE EVIDENCE: 16; original slide associations/timings are unchanged.
ORIGINAL SRT MEDIA EVIDENCE: 949.533; 969.9 seconds; exact spoken wording resides in authoritative SRT, not this synthesis.
SOURCE LINKS [RESEARCH / LINK-OUT ONLY]: https://www.openbible.com/text/john/15-12.htm; https://www.ccel.org/j/jfb/jfb/JFB43.htm

nodes.title: hamartōlos
nodes.summary: Pastor Jacob uses the Lexham Theological Wordbook term hamartōlos in the Romans 5:8 section to describe sinful behavior/condition.
nodes.notes:
LEXICAL REVIEW [Romans 5:8]: Greek inflected ἁμαρτωλῶν is genitive masculine plural of ἁμαρτωλός (G268) with ὄντων (“being”), describing people as sinners while Christ died. Jake’s Lexham-derived “sinful” / behavior gloss is cited external material; broader verse emphasizes their moral state before God. Published Greek interlinear cross-check complete; pinned STEPBible dataset gate remains OPEN.

SPP2 v1.1 ADDITIVE SCRIPTURE RESEARCH | Romans 5:8 | publication status: RESEARCH REVIEW, NOT AUTOMATIC PUBLIC DISPLAY
SOURCE TEXT CONTEXT [INDEPENDENT]: Romans 5:1-11, justification, peace, suffering, hope, and God’s love demonstrated in Christ’s death for the ungodly. Audience/genre: Paul’s letter to Christians at Rome.
INDEPENDENT BIBLICAL ANALYSIS [NOT PASTOR ATTRIBUTION]: ἁμαρτωλῶν is a genitive masculine plural adjective functioning substantively (“sinners”) within a genitive absolute with ὄντων (“while we were sinners”). συνίστησιν (“demonstrates”) emphasizes God’s initiative. The term is not merely a behavioral checklist, nor is its meaning created by the English word “sinner.”
ORIGINAL-LANGUAGE FORMS [PROVISIONAL interlinear cross-check; STEPBible dataset pin OPEN]: Romans 5:8: ἁμαρτωλῶν (lemma ἁμαρτωλός, G268; adjective genitive masculine plural, substantival with ὄντων); Romans 5:8: ὄντων (lemma εἰμί, G1510; present active participle genitive masculine plural)
PASTOR — FAITHFUL AI SYNTHESIS [NOT SPOKEN EXACT]: At 982–1040 s Jake reads the verse, quotes a Lexham-derived definition of hamartōlos, and applies the text to people who think they must fix themselves before coming to Christ.
HISTORICAL COMMENTARY / EXTERNAL COMPARISON [ATTRIBUTED, EDITION/DATASET VERIFICATION OPEN]: JFB/Henry historical witness cross-check may be included, but no verse-specific HelloAO payload/edition was independently pinned in this review.
ASSESSMENT [REVIEW]: SUPPORTED main thrust; QUALIFIED lexical treatment: Jake’s “sinful behavior” captures part of a semantic range, while Romans 5 describes persons’ moral condition before God.
INTERPRETIVE / RIGHTS GATE: Preserve Lexham Theological Wordbook as an attributed external resource, not as Jake’s original Greek analysis.
ORIGINAL PPTX SOURCE SLIDE EVIDENCE: 17; 18; original slide associations/timings are unchanged.
ORIGINAL SRT MEDIA EVIDENCE: 982.149; 1040.1 seconds; exact spoken wording resides in authoritative SRT, not this synthesis.
SOURCE LINKS [RESEARCH / LINK-OUT ONLY]: https://biblehub.com/text/romans/5-8.htm

nodes.title: God's love precedes our cleanup
nodes.text: God loved us before we were even lovable.
nodes.notes:
INDEPENDENT CONTEXT [Romans 5:1–11; Ephesians 2:1–10]: God demonstrates love while the recipients are sinners; in Ephesians God is grammatical actor of συνεζωοποίησεν, “made alive with Christ.” PASTOR SYNTHESIS [982–1204s]: Christ’s love precedes moral cleanup. STATUS SUPPORTED. Do not infer a doctrine from a single English gloss.

SPP2 v1.1 ADDITIVE SCRIPTURE RESEARCH | Ephesians 2:1-5 | publication status: RESEARCH REVIEW, NOT AUTOMATIC PUBLIC DISPLAY
SOURCE TEXT CONTEXT [INDEPENDENT]: Ephesians 2:1-10, from former condition to God’s initiative and salvation by grace; Ephesians 2:11-22 develops Jew–Gentile unity. Audience/genre: Paul to the church at Ephesus and associated believers.
INDEPENDENT BIBLICAL ANALYSIS [NOT PASTOR ATTRIBUTION]: The contrast is “dead” in transgressions versus God making believers alive with Christ. συνεζωοποίησεν is aorist active indicative, third singular: God is grammatical actor. χάριτί (“by grace”) is a dative noun; σεσῳσμένοι is a perfect passive participle with present εστε, emphasizing salvation received with continuing result.
ORIGINAL-LANGUAGE FORMS [PROVISIONAL interlinear cross-check; STEPBible dataset pin OPEN]: Ephesians 2:5: συνεζωοποίησεν (lemma συζωοποιέω, G4806; aorist active indicative 3rd singular); Ephesians 2:5: σεσῳσμένοι (lemma σῴζω, G4982; perfect middle/passive participle nominative masculine plural)
PASTOR — FAITHFUL AI SYNTHESIS [NOT SPOKEN EXACT]: At 1144–1204 s Jake reads the former lost condition and stresses “but God,” then uses the passage to motivate love toward those who have not yet believed.
HISTORICAL COMMENTARY / EXTERNAL COMPARISON [ATTRIBUTED, EDITION/DATASET VERIFICATION OPEN]: Matthew Henry treats 2:1-10 as divine mercy rather than human self-rescue; selected historical witness is supportive but should remain separate from Jake attribution.
ASSESSMENT [REVIEW]: SUPPORTED; note that vv. 1–5 are used in a theological argument about the source of love, not as proof every individual case of correction has the same form.
INTERPRETIVE / RIGHTS GATE: No full NASB95 verse reproduction in the enriched canonical record.
ORIGINAL PPTX SOURCE SLIDE EVIDENCE: 19; 20; 22; original slide associations/timings are unchanged.
ORIGINAL SRT MEDIA EVIDENCE: 1144.333; 1204.0 seconds; exact spoken wording resides in authoritative SRT, not this synthesis.
SOURCE LINKS [RESEARCH / LINK-OUT ONLY]: https://biblehub.com/text/ephesians/2-5.htm

nodes.title: Love does not mean supporting sin
nodes.text: You must love people no matter the condition they are in. This does not mean that we tolerate or support their sins.
nodes.notes: PASTOR SYNTHESIS [1204–1328s]: Loving those in sin need not imply affirming sin; Jake discusses correction, difficult relationships, and love independent of hearer response. INDEPENDENT ANALYSIS [1 Corinthians 13:4–7]: ἀγάπη acts kindly/patiently and rejoices with truth rather than wrongdoing, but no command to correct every person in one manner follows mechanically. STATUS QUALIFIED.

nodes.title: Truth spoken lovingly
nodes.spokenExact: Unconditional love is not afraid of saying the rough truth with a tough truth in a loving way.
nodes.displayText: Unconditional love is not afraid of saying the tough truth in a loving way.
nodes.notes:
Display wording removes the spoken restart while preserving meaning.

INDEPENDENT BIBLICAL COMPARISON [1 Corinthians 12–14]: truth and love are linked in Paul’s moral/communal argument; “rejoices with the truth” is not mere rhetorical permission for directness. JFB/Henry describe active kindness, long-suffering and restraint. PASTOR SYNTHESIS [1258–1361s] preserves Jake’s faithful-truth emphasis.

SPP2 v1.1 ADDITIVE SCRIPTURE RESEARCH | 1 Corinthians 13:4-7 | publication status: RESEARCH REVIEW, NOT AUTOMATIC PUBLIC DISPLAY
SOURCE TEXT CONTEXT [INDEPENDENT]: 1 Corinthians 12–14: spiritual gifts, corporate rivalry, excellence of love, and edification. Audience/genre: Paul to Corinthian congregation in a setting of church tensions.
INDEPENDENT BIBLICAL ANALYSIS [NOT PASTOR ATTRIBUTION]: Love is expressed through multiple present-tense predicates: μακροθυμεῖ (shows patience), χρηστεύεται (acts kindly), and οὐ χαίρει ἐπὶ τῇ ἀδικίᾳ but συγχαίρει τῇ ἀληθείᾳ (does not delight in wrongdoing but rejoices with truth). The contrast concerns moral truth, not license for harshness.
ORIGINAL-LANGUAGE FORMS [PROVISIONAL interlinear cross-check; STEPBible dataset pin OPEN]: 1 Corinthians 13:4: μακροθυμεῖ (lemma μακροθυμέω, G3114; present active indicative 3rd singular); 1 Corinthians 13:4: χρηστεύεται (lemma χρηστεύομαι, G5541; present middle/passive-form indicative 3rd singular)
PASTOR — FAITHFUL AI SYNTHESIS [NOT SPOKEN EXACT]: At 1204–1328 s Jake clarifies that love need not endorse sin, recounts relational pain over correction, and at 1333–1472 s reads Paul’s description and urges intentional love.
HISTORICAL COMMENTARY / EXTERNAL COMPARISON [ATTRIBUTED, EDITION/DATASET VERIFICATION OPEN]: JFB highlights patience with provocations and active kindness; Henry applies the virtues to Corinthian selfishness, restraint of resentment and joy in truth.
ASSESSMENT [REVIEW]: SUPPORTED; distinction: love and truth can coincide, but this passage does not bless any particular rebuke automatically.
INTERPRETIVE / RIGHTS GATE: Avoid translating “believes all things” as credulity; read in relation to sincerity and hope.
ORIGINAL PPTX SOURCE SLIDE EVIDENCE: 23; 24; original slide associations/timings are unchanged.
ORIGINAL SRT MEDIA EVIDENCE: 1203.966; 1472.766 seconds; exact spoken wording resides in authoritative SRT, not this synthesis.

nodes.title: Learn about God increasingly

conceptCandidates.label: Family discipleship
conceptCandidates.reason: The node explicitly extends personal learning responsibility into the home/family context.

nodes.notes:
SCRIPTURE ANALYSIS [Psalm 25 whole]: Hebrew הוֹדִיעֵנִי (H3045 Hiphil imperative), לַמְּדֵנִי (H3925 Piel imperative) and הַדְרִיכֵנִי (H1869 Hiphil imperative) are prayer requests for knowledge, teaching and guidance. PASTOR SYNTHESIS [1475–1710s]: study Scripture personally and teach family. EDITORIAL FLAG: Jake orally says Psalm 24:4–5 at 1654s, while his recitation, slide 26, prepared PDF and canonical reference identify Psalm 25:4–5.

SPP2 v1.1 ADDITIVE SCRIPTURE RESEARCH | Psalm 25:4-5 | publication status: RESEARCH REVIEW, NOT AUTOMATIC PUBLIC DISPLAY
SOURCE TEXT CONTEXT [INDEPENDENT]: Psalm 25 whole acrostic prayer: reliance on God, confession, guidance, covenant mercy and waiting. Audience/genre: Davidic psalm speaking in prayer to YHWH.
INDEPENDENT BIBLICAL ANALYSIS [NOT PASTOR ATTRIBUTION]: הוֹדִיעֵנִי is a Hiphil imperative from ידע, “cause me to know”; לַמְּדֵנִי is a Piel imperative from למד, “teach me”; הַדְרִיכֵנִי is Hiphil imperative from דרך, “guide/lead me.” These requests express prayerful dependence, not merely accumulation of information.
ORIGINAL-LANGUAGE FORMS [PROVISIONAL interlinear cross-check; STEPBible dataset pin OPEN]: Psalm 25:4: הוֹדִיעֵנִי (lemma ידע, H3045; Hiphil imperative masculine singular with 1cs suffix); Psalm 25:4: לַמְּדֵנִי (lemma למד, H3925; Piel imperative masculine singular with 1cs suffix); Psalm 25:5: הַדְרִיכֵנִי (lemma דרך, H1869; Hiphil imperative masculine singular with 1cs suffix)
PASTOR — FAITHFUL AI SYNTHESIS [NOT SPOKEN EXACT]: At 1475–1710 s Jake urges personal/family Scripture study. Around 1654 s he says “Psalm 24:4–5” orally but recites content from Psalm 25:4–5, as the original notes and slide 26 correctly show.
HISTORICAL COMMENTARY / EXTERNAL COMPARISON [ATTRIBUTED, EDITION/DATASET VERIFICATION OPEN]: Independent reading of the Hebrew prayer supports the practical lesson of dependence and teachability; no specific JFB/Henry Psalm entry has been edition/verse verified for this review.
ASSESSMENT [REVIEW]: SUPPORTED core application; verified spoken reference discrepancy. Do not silently edit the original SRT.
INTERPRETIVE / RIGHTS GATE: Document oral Psalm 24 vs actual Psalm 25 source; distinguish Christian home study application from the psalm’s first-person prayer.

nodes.title: Live to share Jesus intentionally
nodes.summary: The third relationship is with the mission: believers are responsible to proclaim the gospel, not only pastors.
nodes.notes:
TEXTUAL GATE [Mark 16:9–20]: the passage is in the traditional longer ending absent from two early complete Greek witnesses and present in other traditions. INDEPENDENT TEXT ANALYSIS [v15]: κηρύξατε (G2784) is a 2pl aorist imperative to the Eleven in this narrative, “proclaim the gospel.” PASTOR SYNTHESIS [1728–1885s]: all believers can share Jesus although not all are pastors. Do not claim that identical church office is grammatically proven by this verse. Matthews 28:18–20 provides another commission text already in this sermon.

SPP2 v1.1 ADDITIVE SCRIPTURE RESEARCH | Mark 16:14-15 | publication status: RESEARCH REVIEW, NOT AUTOMATIC PUBLIC DISPLAY
SOURCE TEXT CONTEXT [INDEPENDENT]: Mark 16:1-8 ends in fear at the tomb in early witnesses; vv. 9-20 is the traditional longer ending in many later witnesses. Audience/genre: Traditional longer-ending narrative: resurrected Jesus addressing the Eleven.
INDEPENDENT BIBLICAL ANALYSIS [NOT PASTOR ATTRIBUTION]: κηρύξατε (aorist active imperative, second plural, κηρύσσω G2784) means proclaim the gospel. It is addressed in its narrative setting to the disciples, not explicitly to every later Christian in identical formal office. The textual status of Mark 16:9–20 is disputed: absent in Codices Sinaiticus/Vaticanus, present in other ancient streams.
ORIGINAL-LANGUAGE FORMS [PROVISIONAL interlinear cross-check; STEPBible dataset pin OPEN]: Mark 16:15: κηρύξατε (lemma κηρύσσω, G2784; aorist active imperative 2nd plural)
PASTOR — FAITHFUL AI SYNTHESIS [NOT SPOKEN EXACT]: At 1728–1788 s Jake reads the longer-ending passage, explains the term with Lexham, distinguishes pastors from believers, and urges every Christian to share Jesus. This is his pastoral application.
HISTORICAL COMMENTARY / EXTERNAL COMPARISON [ATTRIBUTED, EDITION/DATASET VERIFICATION OPEN]: External textual criticism qualifies use of Mark’s longer ending. Matthew 28:18–20 provides an independent, undisputed commissioning passage within Jake’s own sermon.
ASSESSMENT [REVIEW]: QUALIFIED: proclamation is a valid contextual sense; the universal-member-application is a wider theological synthesis, not a direct grammatical result of the second-person plural imperative.
INTERPRETIVE / RIGHTS GATE: Open textual variant gate for Mark 16:9–20; do not misstate manuscript consensus or attribute this research issue to Jake.
ORIGINAL PPTX SOURCE SLIDE EVIDENCE: 27; 28; 29; 30; original slide associations/timings are unchanged.
ORIGINAL SRT MEDIA EVIDENCE: 1715.099; 1885.433 seconds; exact spoken wording resides in authoritative SRT, not this synthesis.
SOURCE LINKS [RESEARCH / LINK-OUT ONLY]: https://biblehub.com/text/mark/16-15.htm; https://www.uncover.org.uk/mark/ask/whats-going-on-with-the-end-of-marks-gospel

nodes.title: kēryssō
nodes.summary: Pastor Jacob uses the Lexham Theological Wordbook term kēryssō to explain preach/proclaim in the Mark 16 section.
nodes.notes: WORD-STUDY RESEARCH: v15 actual verb κηρύξατε, lemma κηρύσσω (G2784), aorist active imperative second plural. Romans 10:14 has κηρύσσοντος (same lemma), present active participle genitive masculine singular. Contextually heralding a public message; not a semantic definition of pastor office. Lexham prepared quotation belongs to the external wordbook. Mark longer-ending text-critical issue remains open.

nodes.title: Every believer is a proclaimer
nodes.spokenExact: Listen, not everyone's a pastor. But everyone's a proclaimer of truth.
nodes.displayText: Not everyone's a pastor. But everyone's a proclaimer of truth.
nodes.notes: PASTOR SYNTHESIS [1747–1785s]: Jake explicitly distinguishes formal pastor from ordinary believer witness and calls every believer a proclaimer. INDEPENDENT ANALYSIS: the specific Mark 16:15 imperative is addressed to the Eleven; applying Christian witness more broadly requires multiple texts and pastoral reasoning. Do not change Jake’s teaching or misrepresent lexical parsing as spoken.

nodes.title: The gospel content
nodes.text: This is what it is to share the good news of Jesus, the gospel, the truth that Jesus lived, died for our sins, and rose again the 3rd day.

nodes.title: Share what Jesus did for you
nodes.text: All you have to share is what Jesus did for you.

nodes.title: Lead others to Christ continually
nodes.summary: The final relationship continues the mission emphasis through the Great Commission and Romans 10.
nodes.notes:
INDEPENDENT ANALYSIS [Matthew 28:16–20]: main imperative μαθητεύσατε (G3100) is “make disciples”; participles include πορευθέντες (“going”), βαπτίζοντες (“baptizing”), διδάσκοντες (“teaching”). In vv18–20 Jesus’ authority and presence frame ongoing disciple formation. PASTOR SYNTHESIS [1889–2074s]: keep leading others to Christ and prioritize reaching people, not a crude size target. QUALIFICATION: the grammatical disciple-formation analysis is research depth, not a claim that Jake expounded these forms aloud.

SPP2 v1.1 ADDITIVE SCRIPTURE RESEARCH | Matthew 28:18-20 | publication status: RESEARCH REVIEW, NOT AUTOMATIC PUBLIC DISPLAY
SOURCE TEXT CONTEXT [INDEPENDENT]: Matthew 28:16-20 after resurrection, on a Galilean mountain, with Jesus’ universal authority and enduring presence framing the charge. Audience/genre: Resurrected Jesus to Eleven disciples (v. 16), with an all-nations horizon.
INDEPENDENT BIBLICAL ANALYSIS [NOT PASTOR ATTRIBUTION]: μαθητεύσατε (aorist active imperative 2pl) is the central command: make disciples. πορευθέντες is an aorist passive-form participle (“going”), while βαπτίζοντες and διδάσκοντες are present active participles spelling out baptizing and teaching to obey. This is deeper than a numeric-conversion program.
ORIGINAL-LANGUAGE FORMS [PROVISIONAL interlinear cross-check; STEPBible dataset pin OPEN]: Matthew 28:19: μαθητεύσατε (lemma μαθητεύω, G3100; aorist active imperative 2nd plural); Matthew 28:19: πορευθέντες (lemma πορεύομαι, G4198; aorist passive-form participle nominative masculine plural); Matthew 28:19: βαπτίζοντες (lemma βαπτίζω, G907; present active participle nominative masculine plural); Matthew 28:20: διδάσκοντες (lemma διδάσκω, G1321; present active participle nominative masculine plural)
PASTOR — FAITHFUL AI SYNTHESIS [NOT SPOKEN EXACT]: At 1889–1920 s Jake reads the commission, stresses leading others to Christ, and later rejects apathy toward reaching the lost while explicitly recognizing small churches may still be faithful.
HISTORICAL COMMENTARY / EXTERNAL COMPARISON [ATTRIBUTED, EDITION/DATASET VERIFICATION OPEN]: JFB/Henry focus on Christ-given authority and the broad mission; grammar/interpretation cross-check by NET Bible’s passage note supports the central imperative distinction.
ASSESSMENT [REVIEW]: SUPPORTED evangelistic emphasis; ADDITIONAL INDEPENDENT BIBLICAL DEPTH: nurture and teaching are essential components of the Great Commission that Jake reads but does not extensively develop in this sermon.
INTERPRETIVE / RIGHTS GATE: Do not ascribe the Greek-participle analysis or a detailed discipleship model to Jake as though spoken.

nodes.text: The more people come to know Christ, the more people will come to know Christ.

nodes.title: Dead church / risen Savior
nodes.text: How can you be a dead church serving a risen savior?

nodes.title: Salvation is not work-based
nodes.text: We complicate salvation so much that we put all these parameters and all these things that we have to do. Listen, that's work based. Faith-based is God save me. I can do nothing.
nodes.notes: PASTOR SYNTHESIS [2074–2099s]: Jake contrasts salvation through trusting Christ with reliance on works. INDEPENDENT CONTEXT: Rom 10:8–13 presents righteousness through faith and calling upon the Lord; do not remove v13 from the surrounding argument about Christ and Israel.

nodes.title: When did you last bring the good news?
nodes.text: When's the last time you brought the good news?
nodes.notes:
INDEPENDENT CONTEXT [Romans 10:13–17]: Paul reasons backwards from calling on the Lord to faith, hearing, proclamation and sending, also discussing gospel reception by Israel and Gentiles. Jake’s spoken question around 2126s asks when a listener last shared the gospel. Distinguish direct transcript question from newly generated Discover questions.

SPP2 v1.1 ADDITIVE SCRIPTURE RESEARCH | Romans 10:13-15 | publication status: RESEARCH REVIEW, NOT AUTOMATIC PUBLIC DISPLAY
SOURCE TEXT CONTEXT [INDEPENDENT]: Romans 9–11 on Israel, the righteousness of faith, accessibility of salvation and the message sent to Jews and Gentiles; connect Rom 10:8-17. Audience/genre: Paul instructing Christians in Rome.
INDEPENDENT BIBLICAL ANALYSIS [NOT PASTOR ATTRIBUTION]: ἐπικαλέσηται (aorist middle subjunctive 3sg, ἐπικαλέω G1941) in v. 13 conveys whoever calls; ἀκούσωσιν (“may hear,” aorist active subjunctive 3pl) and κηρύσσοντος (present active participle genitive singular, κηρύσσω G2784) are part of a rhetorical dependence chain: call, believe, hear, proclamation, sending. Paul quotes Joel 2:32 in v. 13 and Isaiah 52:7 in v. 15.
ORIGINAL-LANGUAGE FORMS [PROVISIONAL interlinear cross-check; STEPBible dataset pin OPEN]: Romans 10:13: ἐπικαλέσηται (lemma ἐπικαλέω, G1941; aorist middle subjunctive 3rd singular); Romans 10:14: κηρύσσοντος (lemma κηρύσσω, G2784; present active participle genitive masculine singular)
PASTOR — FAITHFUL AI SYNTHESIS [NOT SPOKEN EXACT]: At 2074–2182 s Jake contrasts grace with works, then asks when listeners last proclaimed good news and leaves them with obedience rather than control of hearer response.
HISTORICAL COMMENTARY / EXTERNAL COMPARISON [ATTRIBUTED, EDITION/DATASET VERIFICATION OPEN]: JFB emphasizes that calling presupposes faith, hearing, proclamation and being sent, applied to the legitimacy of the apostolic mission among Gentiles; broader contemporary application should not erase that argument.
ASSESSMENT [REVIEW]: SUPPORTED evangelism application, qualified with Paul’s Jew/Gentile salvation context and the sending motif.
INTERPRETIVE / RIGHTS GATE: Do not reduce Romans 10:13 to an isolated slogan, or claim an ordinary lexical gloss by itself determines Paul’s gospel theology.
ORIGINAL PPTX SOURCE SLIDE EVIDENCE: 36; 37; 38; original slide associations/timings are unchanged.
ORIGINAL SRT MEDIA EVIDENCE: 2073.55; 2182.449 seconds; exact spoken wording resides in authoritative SRT, not this synthesis.
SOURCE LINKS [RESEARCH / LINK-OUT ONLY]: https://biblehub.com/text/romans/10-13.htm; https://biblehub.com/text/romans/10-14.htm; https://www.christianity.com/bible/commentary/jamieson-faussett-brown/romans/10

nodes.title: Our responsibility is obedience
nodes.text: Listen, how other people receive the good news is not up to us. We can let God handle that. What's up to us? Are we gonna do what God has commanded or not?
nodes.notes: PASTOR SYNTHESIS [2166–2182s]: listeners are accountable for obedient gospel witness, while the hearer’s reception is not fully under their control. INDEPENDENT ANALYSIS: Romans 10:13–15 stresses dependence of faith on hearing and the sending of a herald, not numerical outcomes. JFB explicitly relates the logic to Gentile mission.

recurringTheses.statement: Christ must be the foundation before church values, methods, growth, or identity can be rightly ordered.
Christian love is not conditioned on the recipient's response, but it also does not require supporting sin.
Believers carry personal responsibility for growth in Scripture; gathered church teaching cannot replace daily learning.
Ordinary believers are responsible to proclaim the gospel, not merely professional pastors.
Church growth matters when its aim is more people knowing Christ, not growth as an end in itself.

discover.question: Why does the sermon establish Christ as the foundation before introducing Relationships?
discover.answer: Because the vision, mission, and core values only stand rightly when Jesus Christ is the church's foundation and Lord.

discover.question: What is the Relationships core value?
discover.answer: Build and grow the four relationships represented in the church's purpose statement.

discover.question: What does it mean to love others unconditionally?
discover.answer: Love them in the condition they are in.

discover.question: Does unconditional love mean tolerating sin?
discover.answer: No. The sermon distinguishes loving a person from supporting sin and says difficult truth can be spoken lovingly.

discover.question: Who is responsible for a believer's growth in God's Word?
discover.answer: The church teaches, but believers cannot outsource the personal responsibility to learn God's Word and teach their families.

discover.question: What happens when we increasingly learn about God?
discover.answer: The sermon argues that genuine increasing knowledge of God does not leave a person unchanged.

discover.question: Is gospel proclamation only the pastor's responsibility?
discover.answer: No. Not everyone is a pastor, but every believer is called to proclaim the truth of the gospel.

discover.question: What can an ordinary believer share?
discover.answer: What Jesus did for you, anchored in the biblical gospel.

discover.question: How do the four Relationships commitments move outward?
discover.answer: They culminate in the mission to make disciples, proclaim the good news, and lead others to Christ continually.

discover.question: Who controls how people respond to the gospel?
discover.answer: The sermon places the listener's responsibility on faithful obedience and leaves the hearer's response to God.

discover.question: Why is Jesus central to the church’s foundation, and where does Peter fit?
discover.answer: Jake teaches that Christ and the confession of Christ as Lord determine the church’s foundation. Matthew 16:18 addresses Peter directly and uses rock wordplay; scholars differ about whether the image refers especially to Peter, his confession or Christ. That distinction belongs in optional biblical-analysis depth, not as words attributed to Jake.
discover.answerOrigin: ANALYSIS — SYNTHESIS from Pastor Jacob sermon evidence; independent biblical qualifications distinguished in answer

discover.question: Can we love someone without affirming everything they do?
discover.answer: Jake contrasts loving people in their actual condition with endorsing their sin. He draws on Jesus’ self-giving love, God’s grace toward sinners and Paul’s description of patient love that rejoices with truth. His concrete correction advice remains pastoral application, not an automatic mandate for every case.
discover.answerOrigin: ANALYSIS — SYNTHESIS from Pastor Jacob sermon evidence; independent biblical qualifications distinguished in answer

discover.question: What is David asking God to do in Psalm 25?
discover.answer: The psalmist asks God to teach, make known and guide him in truth. Jake applies that prayer to developing personal and family habits of studying Scripture. The spoken “Psalm 24” reference is a miscitation; the recited passage and slide identify Psalm 25:4–5.
discover.answerOrigin: ANALYSIS — SYNTHESIS from Pastor Jacob sermon evidence; independent biblical qualifications distinguished in answer

discover.question: What is the difference between proclaiming and being a pastor?
discover.answer: Jake says not every Christian is a pastor, but believers should share Christ. The Greek verb translated “preach” means proclaim or herald in Mark 16:15. Its original audience is the Eleven and the traditional longer ending is textually disputed, so a broader congregational application should be supported from the whole New Testament witness.
discover.answerOrigin: ANALYSIS — SYNTHESIS from Pastor Jacob sermon evidence; independent biblical qualifications distinguished in answer

discover.question: Does the Great Commission stop when someone makes a decision?
discover.answer: Jake urges leading people to Christ. Matthew 28:18–20 calls for making disciples, including baptizing and teaching them to obey Jesus. The latter observation extends the listener’s biblical study beyond what Jake specifically expounded in his sermon.
discover.answerOrigin: ANALYSIS — SYNTHESIS from Pastor Jacob sermon evidence; independent biblical qualifications distinguished in answer

discover.question: Why does Romans 10 link sending, preaching, hearing and belief?
discover.answer: Paul shows that calling on the Lord depends on believing, hearing a proclaimed message and someone being sent. Jake applies this to practical gospel witness and obedience, while leaving the response of hearers in God’s hands.
discover.answerOrigin: ANALYSIS — SYNTHESIS from Pastor Jacob sermon evidence; independent biblical qualifications distinguished in answer
